title: Draw the map before you pick a metric
brief: A team asks how it will know the assistant works. The stage, the traffic, the risk and the label budget are all unspecified. Decide which checks run where, when they run and what they are allowed to cost.

blocks.md:
Every evaluation answers three questions. **Unit**: do you score one component (retriever, tool selector, judge) or the whole path? **Time**: do you run before release against a fixed set, or after release against live traffic? **Reference**: do you hold an expected answer, or only the question and the output?

Foundry frames the lifecycle as base model selection, pre-production evaluation and post-production monitoring [[r1]]. LangSmith draws the same line from the data side: offline runs use dataset examples that carry reference outputs, while online runs score production traces that have none [[r29]]. Capability evals start at a low pass rate and ask what the agent can do at all. Regression evals should sit near 100% and guard what already works [[r17]].

blocks.title: Where each check lives in the lifecycle
blocks.alt: A loop from model selection to pre-production evaluation, release, post-production monitoring and failing traces that feed back into the pre-production set.
blocks.src:
flowchart LR
  M["Choose base model"] --> P["Pre-production evals"]
  P --> G["CI gate"]
  G --> R["Release"]
  R --> O["Post-production monitoring"]
  O --> T["Failing traces"]
  T --> P
blocks.caption: Pre-production holds the golden set, red team scans and the CI gate. Foundry lists post-production monitoring as operational metrics, continuous evaluation, scheduled evaluation, scheduled red teaming and Azure Monitor alerts.

blocks.title: Four layers, four jobs
blocks.intro: These layers stack. The question is which one carries the most weight for your dials.

options.name: Component evals
options.summary: Score one stage alone: retriever ranking, tool selection, parser output, the judge itself.
pros: A failure points at one stage
Mostly deterministic or cheap, so it runs on every commit
cons: Parts can pass while the whole path fails
Needs labels at the stage boundary, such as relevant chunk ids
options.bestWhen: You change one stage often, or a regression must be localized in minutes.
options.avoidWhen: It is your only check, because interactions between stages stay invisible.

options.name: End-to-end offline suite
options.summary: Run golden tasks through the full system and grade the outcome.
pros: Tests the path users actually take
Gives a stable baseline for a release gate
cons: Judge calls multiply: items x evaluators x trials
A drop does not say which stage moved
options.bestWhen: Before every release and after any prompt, model or tool change.
options.avoidWhen: You need to know why it failed and have no component scores beside it.

options.name: Online sampled scoring
options.summary: Score a sample of live traces with reference-free judges and safety evaluators, off the request path.
pros: Scoring logged traces adds no user-facing latency
cons: Detects problems after users saw the answer
Judge tokens per trace, so sampling and caps control spend
Reads real content, so privacy rules apply
options.bestWhen: Traffic exists and you need drift and safety coverage.
options.avoidWhen: You are pre-launch, or it is the only guard on high-harm output.

options.name: Expert trace review
options.summary: A named domain expert reads sampled traces and writes pass/fail verdicts with critiques.
pros: Finds failure types no metric names yet
Produces the labels that calibrate judges
cons: Slowest and most expensive per item
Reviewers drift without a shared rubric
options.bestWhen: Outputs are high-harm, or you need labels to calibrate a judge.
options.avoidWhen: Volume is high and errors are cheap to undo.

blocks.title: Pick the evaluation mix
blocks.prompt: Flip the constraints. The ranking shows which layer carries the most weight, and why.

options.name: Component evals
options.summary: Score retriever, tool selection and parsers alone.

options.name: End-to-end golden suite
options.summary: Whole-path tasks as a release gate.

options.name: Expert trace review
options.summary: A named reviewer reads sampled traces.

options.name: Shadow run
options.summary: Score a candidate on mirrored live requests.

pre.why: Runs on synthetic and hand-written cases, so no traffic is needed.

live.why: Still localizes a regression, though live traces show more.

low.why: Cheap, narrow checks are enough when mistakes are cheap.

high.why: Necessary but not sufficient, because parts can pass while the whole path fails.

tight.why: Mostly code checks and rank metrics, with little judge spend.

ample.why: Keeps its value, but extra budget buys more elsewhere.

pre.why: The only way to test the whole path before users do.

live.why: Still the release gate, kept fresh by failing production traces.

low.why: Worth having, though not urgent when errors are cheap.

high.why: Whole-path failures such as a wrong tool sequence only show up here.

tight.why: Items x evaluators x trials adds up in judge calls.

ample.why: Affords more trials and harder cases.

pre.why: There is no traffic to sample.

live.why: Real queries, and judge scorers need no reference answers.

low.why: A cheap way to spot drift.

high.why: It detects problems after users saw them, so it cannot be the only guard.

tight.why: Every scored trace costs judge tokens. Sampling is the control.

ample.why: Allows a higher sampling rate and more scorers.

pre.why: Few real traces exist, so reviewers read synthetic rows at best.

live.why: Reading real traces finds failures no metric names.

low.why: Expert time is wasted on cheap mistakes.

high.why: A named reviewer is accountable for high-stakes output.

tight.why: Expert hours are the scarcest budget.

ample.why: Reviews also produce the labels that calibrate judges.

pre.why: Needs a live baseline and traffic to mirror.

live.why: Real requests, and users never see the candidate.

low.why: A direct rollout may be fine, so the extra safety buys little.

high.why: Users never see the candidate's answers, so a bad version costs nothing.

tight.why: It doubles inference on mirrored traffic and adds scoring.

ample.why: Allows mirroring a larger share of traffic.

blocks.takeaway: No layer wins on every dial. Say which dial drove your pick, then say which layer you would add next.

items.symptom: The score fell 6 points and nobody knows which stage moved
items.fix: Add component scores at each stage boundary (ranked chunks, tool selection, judge agreement) and log them in the same run.

items.symptom: The offline suite is green while production quality falls
items.cause: The golden set stopped matching real queries
items.fix: Sample failing production traces into the golden set on a schedule, tag them by origin, and watch online scores for drift.

items.symptom: Every release is blocked by a suite that never passes
items.cause: Capability tasks sit inside the release gate
items.fix: Gate on regression and safety suites. Keep capability suites advisory until their tasks graduate.

items.symptom: Online dashboards look healthy and users disagree
items.cause: The reference-free judge was never compared with human labels
items.fix: Sample traces for expert review, compare verdicts with the judge, and recalibrate before trusting the dashboard.

blocks.title: Preview status, checked 2026-10-13

items.title: Go deeper: the OpenAI Evals shutdown

blocks.md: OpenAI announced on 2026-06-03 that the Evals platform is deprecated. Existing evals become read-only on 2026-10-31, and the dashboard and API are scheduled to shut down on 2026-11-30. Graders documented for eval workflows are part of the transition, and OpenAI points to Promptfoo as the migration path [[r19]].

Export what you need and move to a code-first harness. The Learn pages checked on 2026-10-13 show no matching retirement notice for Azure OpenAI graders, so treat the effect on Foundry's OpenAI-style evaluation API as unconfirmed. The judge and dataset advice in OpenAI's guide still holds [[r18]].

quiz.q: After a retriever swap the end-to-end pass rate fell 6 points, and nobody can say whether retrieval or generation is at fault. Which earlier choice would have located the fault fastest?
options: Add several hundred more golden tasks, scored only end to end, to tighten the interval
Switch to a stronger judge model for the final answer
Score the ranked chunks with a retrieval evaluation before generation runs
Lower the generator temperature so runs repeat
quiz.explain: A separate retrieval score shows whether the ranked chunks changed, which splits the fault between retrieval and generation. More end-to-end tasks tighten the interval but still give one number for the whole path. A stronger judge improves how the answer is graded, not where the fault sits. Lower temperature reduces run-to-run noise but does not localize a regression.

quiz.q: Select every statement about online evaluation of live traffic that holds.
options: Production traces carry no reference outputs, so it leans on reference-free judges and safety checks
Scoring can run asynchronously on logged traces without adding user-facing latency
It makes the offline golden set unnecessary because live queries are more realistic
Sampling rate and filters are the main lever on judge cost
quiz.explain: Live traces have no expected answer, so online scoring uses reference-free judges and safety checks [[r29]]. Braintrust scores logged traces asynchronously with no latency impact [[r30]]. Judge tokens scale with the number of scored traces, so sampling is the cost control. The third statement fails: online scoring cannot run reference-based metrics or gate a release against a fixed baseline, so the offline set stays.

quiz.q: Put the evaluation feedback loop in order.
items: Run the suite as a release gate
Release and score sampled live traffic
Add failing production traces to the golden set
Rerun the gate on the enlarged set
quiz.explain: Cases come first because the gate needs something to run. Release and live scoring follow the gate. Failing traces only exist after live scoring, and the enlarged set is what the next gate run uses. This is the loop Foundry draws between pre-production evaluation and post-production monitoring.

takeaways: Name the unit, the timing and the reference before you name a metric.
Component scores localize a fault. End-to-end scores say whether users are affected. You need both.
Offline sets gate releases, online scoring watches drift, and failing traces flow back into the offline set.
Capability suites stay advisory. Regression and safety suites block the release.
Label every preview feature with its date and keep a code-first fallback.
